power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: As power analysis for mediation analyses with nested data is not readily available in G*Power or any other standard software, we relied on simulation study findings by Pan et al. (2018), which indicated a necessary sample size of N = 465 to achieve a power of .80, assuming small effects for both a-and b-paths of the mediation and an intraclass correlation coefficient of .87 (as observed in Study 1). Hence, we recruited 502 participants (47.8% female, 49.8% male, 2.4% other; Mage = 42.8, SDage = 12.7; 6.0% Asian, 3.6% Black, 4.6% mixed, and 82.9% White in terms of ethnicity). As preregistered, we excluded incomplete responses (n = 6) as well as participants who failed attention checks (n = 49) from all analyses, leading to a final sample size of N = 447.
table.effect_size_metric_other: small effects for a- and b-paths of the mediation

table.text: Across two studies, we investigated whether people are curious about others' life stories, whether this curiosity depends on the story's valence or the cultural distance to its protagonist, and if so why. Consistently, we found that stories about negative life events (e.g., death, illness, financial loss) elicited more curiosity than stories about positive life events (e.g., birth, marriage, career progression), and that curiosity peaked for negative stories about culturally close others. With higher power in Study 2, we also uncovered a main effect of cultural distance such that people generally experienced more curiosity for stories about culturally close rather than distant others (a post-hoc power analysis indicated that Study 1 was underpowered with only 25% power to detect an effect of such size). Finally, Study 2 indicated that people were more curious about negative stories, as they anticipated to gain more insight and to feel greater distress through engaging with these stories. Combined, these mediating pathways outweighed a simultaneous counteracting path that attenuated curiosity for negative stories via lower enjoyment, with all three together fully explaining the valencecuriosity relationship. Thus, expectations of greater insight and distress can be interpreted as 'pull factors', which increase people's curiosity for negative stories about others' experiences.

In Study 1, we manipulated story valence and cultural distance to measure how these variables impact curiosity about others' stories. Following a 2 (positive versus negative valence) x 2 (high versus low cultural distance) within-subject design, we fully counterbalanced all aspects of the design across a total of 36 trials (9 per condition) per participant (see Supplemental Figure 1). Participants were restricted to be aged 18-65, located in the UK, with English as their first language and with a submission-quality rejection rate of below 5 percent across their previous research participations on Prolific. Additionally, an equal gender ratio was ensured. With no previous data on which to base the effect size assumptions, we assessed the sample size required for a within-factor repeated-measures ANOVA to detect a small effect of f(U) = 0.2 with high power (.95) at a 5% level of significance using G*Power (Version 3.1, Faul et al., 2007), which was 146. Following this, we recruited 149 participants (49.7% female, 49.7% male, 0.7% other; Mage = 39.2, SDage = 13.5; 6.7% Asian, 4.7% Black, 2.7% mixed, and 81.2% White in terms of ethnicity) through Prolific.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .05", Text = "No significant differences were found between the other conditions (ps > .05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. table.formatted: We did not observe a main effect for cultural distance on curiosity, b = -1.16, t(149) = -1.49, p = .138, 95% CI = [-2.68, 0.37], but a significant interaction between valence and cultural distance, b = 2.70, t(149) = 2.34, p = .021, 95% CI = [0.42, 4.99], see Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>.
table.expanded: We did not observe a main effect for cultural distance on curiosity, b = -1.16, t(149) = -1.49, p = .138, 95% CI = [-2.68, 0.37], but a significant interaction between valence and cultural distance, b = 2.70, t(149) = 2.34, p = .021, 95% CI = [0.42, 4.99], see Figure 2.

table.formatted: No significant differences were found between the other conditions (ps > .05).
table.expanded: No significant differences were found between the other conditions (ps > .05).

After accounting for the above three indirect effects, valence did not directly link to curiosity anymore, b = -2.54, p = .062, 95% CI [-5.22, 0.13], which indicates that greater anticipated insight and -counterintuitively at first sight -greater anticipated distress fully account for higher curiosity observed for negative stories.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .138", "ps > .05", "p = .062"), Sentence = c("We did not observe a main effect for cultural distance on curiosity, b = -1.16, t(149) = -1.49, p = .138, 95% CI = [-2.68, 0.37], but a significant interaction between valence and cultural distance, b = 2.70, t(149) = 2.34, p = .021, 95% CI = [0.42, 4.99], see Figure 2.", "No significant differences were found between the other conditions (ps > .05).", "After accounting for the above three indirect effects, valence did not directly link to curiosity anymore, b = -2.54, p = .062, 95% CI [-5.22, 0.13], which indicates that greater anticipated insight and -counterintuitively at first sight -greater anticipated distress fully account for higher curiosity observed for negative stories." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. #### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 4 spreadsheet files in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("S1_materialbook.xlsx", "S1_materialbook.xlsx", 
"S1_materialbook.xlsx"), Sheet = c("countries", "countries", 
"countries"), Issue = c("Colour coding", "Empty rows", "Empty or unnamed columns"
), Detail = c("36 cells use fill colour to encode information; colour is lost on CSV export.", 
"2 fully empty rows inside the data range.", "4 columns are empty or have a blank header."
)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were restricted to be aged 18-65, located in the UK, with English as their first language and with a submission-quality rejection rate of below 5 percent across their previous research participations on Prolific.

Following this, we recruited 149 participants (49.7% female, 49.7% male, 0.7% other; Mage = 39.2, SDage = 13.5; 6.7% Asian, 4.7% Black, 2.7% mixed, and 81.2% White in terms of ethnicity) through Prolific.

Participants were shown headlines describing positive or negative life stories about other people, along with maps indicating the country of origin (high or low in cultural distance) of the story's protagonist.
After rating all the stories, the headlines were displayed again, and participants were asked to rate the story's valence and the cultural distance of the protagonist (see Figure 1).
Participants were not provided with the actual stories.
Finally, participants filled out the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR, Kashdan et al., 2020), included for exploratory purposes, and provided demographical information (gender, age).
Study 1 was approved by the ethical committee of the second author's institution; all participants gave informed consent.

To counterbalance potential country-or storyspecific effects, participants were randomly assigned to one of four combination sets, which varied the country-story-pairings (for a visualization, see Supplemental Figure 1).

Participants were recruited via Prolific, using the same sample restrictions as in Study 1 except for controlling for UK nationality rather than restricting first language to English, as to further strengthen the cultural distance manipulation.
Hence, we recruited 502 participants (47.8% female, 49.8% male, 2.4% other; Mage = 42.8, SDage = 12.7; 6.0% Asian, 3.6% Black, 4.6% mixed, and 82.9% White in terms of ethnicity).

In addition, after having rated their curiosity for all stories in the first part of the study, participants were presented with each headline (including country of origin) again and asked to indicate their agreement with six statements regarding the predicted impact of reading the story (see Table 1 and Figure 3).
Study 2 was approved by the ethical committee of the first author's institution; all participants gave informed consent.

To vary cultural distance within our stimuli, stories presented to participants were described as either stemming from a country with low or high cultural distance to the UK, according to Muthukrishna and colleagues' (2020) cultural distance indicator.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false

    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------

```

text.text: Personalized stories about others' life experiences are omnipresent in media, yet we know little about what drives people to engage with such narratives.

Across two studies (N = 596 UK adults), we investigated how valence (positive versus negative life event) and cultural distance (experience from someone from a culturally close versus distant country) shape social curiosity.
Consistently, participants reported greater curiosity for stories about negative life events, especially when the story's protagonist was culturally close.

Structural equation modelling revealed that the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity was mediated through greater anticipated insight and -counterintuitive at first sight -greater anticipated distress towards negative stories.
At the same time, curiosity for negative stories was attenuated through lower expected enjoyment.
These findings suggest that curiosity is driven by anticipated emotional impact of either valence, and have implications for fostering empathy and meaningful engagement in media and public discourse.
experiences -also referred to as 'soft news' (Reinemann et al., 2012) -are omnipresent in today's media landscape.
text.formatted: experiences -also referred to as 'soft news' <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Reinemann et al., 2012)</ref> -are omnipresent in today's media landscape.

text.text: Be it through formats such as above, or through documentaries, podcasts, or social media stories: people frequently engage with others' life narratives (Aroesti, 2023).
text.formatted: Be it through formats such as above, or through documentaries, podcasts, or social media stories: people frequently engage with others' life narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aroesti, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While engaging with these stories is common, little is known about when and why people are curious to learn about others' experiences.
Compared to traditional avenues in curiosity research, such as on perceptual and epistemic curiosity (Berlyne, 1954; Loewenstein, 1994), research on social curiosity has been limited.
text.formatted: Compared to traditional avenues in curiosity research, such as on perceptual and epistemic curiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Berlyne, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Loewenstein, 1994)</ref>, research on social curiosity has been limited.

text.text: Social curiosity is defined as an interest in acquiring information about how others behave, think, and feel (Litman & Pezzo, 2007; Renner, 2006).
text.formatted: Social curiosity is defined as an interest in acquiring information about how others behave, think, and feel <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Litman & Pezzo, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Renner, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Early work on social or interpersonal curiosity was focused on the interest in factual, externally verifiable information about people's lives (Singer & Antrobus, 1963).
text.formatted: Early work on social or interpersonal curiosity was focused on the interest in factual, externally verifiable information about people's lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Singer & Antrobus, 1963)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, this grew to include curiosity about internal experiences, such as people's emotions and thoughts (Litman & Pezzo, 2007; Renner, 2006).
text.formatted: Over time, this grew to include curiosity about internal experiences, such as people's emotions and thoughts <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Litman & Pezzo, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Renner, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Note that in the way we define curiosity in the present work, the emphasis lies on the type of content that people are curious about (i.e., social information) and not on the behavior through which curiosity is expressed (i.e., interpersonal interaction).

To date, most existing work on social curiosity has taken a trait perspective (Hartung & Renner, 2013; Kashdan et al., 2020), conceptualizing social curiosity as an enduring motivation to explore information about other people (Renner, 2006; Silva, 2019).
text.formatted: To date, most existing work on social curiosity has taken a trait perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hartung & Renner, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kashdan et al., 2020)</ref>, conceptualizing social curiosity as an enduring motivation to explore information about other people <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Renner, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Silva, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Situationally triggered, state-like expressions of social curiosity, however, remain largely unexplored.
As a result, we know little about which contextual factors and situational motives influence curiosity experienced in response to social information about others in the moment.

Yet, understanding what encourages people to engage with others' narratives and perspectives, particularly when these may be challenging to hear, bears important implications for NGOs and charities (i.e., enhancing pro-social behavior; Bagozzi & Moore, 1994), politics and social media (i.e., managing polarization; Saveski et al., 2022), and journalism and the news (i.e., managing healthy news consumption; Gottfried, 2020).
text.formatted: Yet, understanding what encourages people to engage with others' narratives and perspectives, particularly when these may be challenging to hear, bears important implications for NGOs and charities (i.e., enhancing pro-social behavior; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bagozzi & Moore, 1994)</ref>, politics and social media (i.e., managing polarization; <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Saveski et al., 2022)</ref>, and journalism and the news (i.e., managing healthy news consumption; <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Gottfried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We addressed this gap by focusing on two situational predictors of social curiosity: valence and cultural distance.
We investigate curiosity for others' life stories depending on whether the events described are positive or negative, and whether the protagonist is culturally close or distant to the reader.

Specifically, we test the idea that people are generally more curious about negative as opposed to positive experiences, and that this difference is particularly pronounced for stories about culturally close others.
Traditionally, much of situational curiosity research has studied positive or neutral stimuli, such as trivia questions or novel, interesting facts (Gruber & Ranganath, 2019; Loewenstein, 1994).
text.formatted: Traditionally, much of situational curiosity research has studied positive or neutral stimuli, such as trivia questions or novel, interesting facts <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gruber & Ranganath, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Loewenstein, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This approach aligns with the idea that humans are generally driven to seek out positive and avoid negative affect (Elliot, 2006; Kahneman et al., 1999).
text.formatted: This approach aligns with the idea that humans are generally driven to seek out positive and avoid negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Elliot, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kahneman et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: However, this hedonic perspective on curiosity contrasts with everyday reality, where engagement with negative content is a common phenomenon.

Most news is negative (Lengauer et al., 2012; Trussler & Soroka, 2014), and negative news tends to receive more attention than positive news (Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020; Robertson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Most news is negative <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lengauer et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Trussler & Soroka, 2014)</ref>, and negative news tends to receive more attention than positive news <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Robertson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Podcasts and documentaries often center around negative experiences, with true crime being one of the most popular genres (Ghosh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Podcasts and documentaries often center around negative experiences, with true crime being one of the most popular genres <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ghosh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, empirical research has shown that people are almost equally likely to approach or to avoid negative content when given the option, and that this likelihood increases when information emphasizes social interaction or personal accounts (Niehoff et al., 2024; Oosterwijk, 2017).
text.formatted: In fact, empirical research has shown that people are almost equally likely to approach or to avoid negative content when given the option, and that this likelihood increases when information emphasizes social interaction or personal accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Niehoff et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Oosterwijk, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The above findings suggest that people frequently experience curiosity for negative content.

Considering the general assumption that people seek positive affect and avoid negative affect (Elliot, 2006; Kahneman et al., 1999), the most straightforward explanation for this behavior is that people simply enjoy the negative -and some have argued so.
text.formatted: Considering the general assumption that people seek positive affect and avoid negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Elliot, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kahneman et al., 1999)</ref>, the most straightforward explanation for this behavior is that people simply enjoy the negative -and some have argued so.

text.text: Rozin and colleagues showed that aversive experiences such as pain, disgust, or sad movies and music can be enjoyed (Rozin et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Rozin and colleagues showed that aversive experiences such as pain, disgust, or sad movies and music can be enjoyed <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Rozin et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Others have discussed the pleasure of negative gossip (Beersma & Van Kleef, 2012), or positive affect through downward comparisons towards others' misfortunes (e.g., Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020; Ouwerkerk et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Others have discussed the pleasure of negative gossip <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Beersma & Van Kleef, 2012)</ref>, or positive affect through downward comparisons towards others' misfortunes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Ouwerkerk et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, a growing body of work suggests that curiosity for negative content may be explained by motives other than sensation seeking or enjoyment (see Niehoff & Oosterwijk, 2020).
text.formatted: However, a growing body of work suggests that curiosity for negative content may be explained by motives other than sensation seeking or enjoyment (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Niehoff & Oosterwijk, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Negative content is perceived as offering high informational value, due to the fact that it is often novel, complex, and deviant from the norm (Alves et al., 2017; Raney et al., 2022) -characteristics that have been well established as drivers of epistemic and perceptual curiosity (Berlyne, 1960).
text.formatted: Negative content is perceived as offering high informational value, due to the fact that it is often novel, complex, and deviant from the norm <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alves et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Raney et al., 2022)</ref> -characteristics that have been well established as drivers of epistemic and perceptual curiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Berlyne, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: As such, negative information may elicit a particularly large knowledge gap and hence a strong deprivation-type drive to reduce uncertainty (Litman, 2005; Litman & Jimerson, 2004).
text.formatted: As such, negative information may elicit a particularly large knowledge gap and hence a strong deprivation-type drive to reduce uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Litman, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Litman & Jimerson, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, research on gossip suggests that negative social information carries reputational information important for cooperation (Dores Cruz, 2024) and is well suited for norm-learning and vicarious observational learning, as lessons can be learned without experiencing negative outcomes firsthand (Baumeister et al., 2004; Hartung et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, research on gossip suggests that negative social information carries reputational information important for cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dores Cruz, 2024)</ref> and is well suited for norm-learning and vicarious observational learning, as lessons can be learned without experiencing negative outcomes firsthand <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Baumeister et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hartung et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, stories about others' negative experiences may also be rewarding as they prompt deep reflection, support the development of a realistic model of the world, and enhance perceptions of self-efficacy (Blain & Sharot, 2021; Murayama et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Moreover, stories about others' negative experiences may also be rewarding as they prompt deep reflection, support the development of a realistic model of the world, and enhance perceptions of self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Blain & Sharot, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Murayama et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, engaging with negative experiences of others carries high emotional costs, such as distress or discomfort (de Bruin et al., 2021).
text.formatted: At the same time, engaging with negative experiences of others carries high emotional costs, such as distress or discomfort <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(de Bruin et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Negative information is known to negatively impact affect and subsequent behavior more strongly and more long-lasting than positive information (Baumeister et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Negative information is known to negatively impact affect and subsequent behavior more strongly and more long-lasting than positive information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Baumeister et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, choosing how to interact with negative information requires a careful weighing of motives that promote or hinder engagement (Niehoff & Oosterwijk, 2020).
text.formatted: Hence, choosing how to interact with negative information requires a careful weighing of motives that promote or hinder engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Niehoff & Oosterwijk, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A favorable cost-to-benefit ratio is crucial for deciding to engage with negative experiences, and any factors that influence this ratio may either increase or decrease curiosity for such content.
We argue that one such factor is the cultural distance to the protagonist of the story.
The cultural distance between two societies can be understood as the size of their psychological differences, such as norms, attitudes, beliefs and behaviors (Muthukrishna et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The cultural distance between two societies can be understood as the size of their psychological differences, such as norms, attitudes, beliefs and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Muthukrishna et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As such, when cued with information about another person, the perceived cultural distance to them may impact curiosity about that person.
Empirical data from a review of 23,000 bilateral state relationships found that countries appeared more often in other countries' news when their cultures were closer (Scherer et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Empirical data from a review of 23,000 bilateral state relationships found that countries appeared more often in other countries' news when their cultures were closer <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Scherer et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, in the same way that most news is negative, most news concerns people or places that are culturally close.

Construal Level Theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010) may explain why this is the case, by proposing that information stemming from people that feel psychologically closer may be processed in more concrete and less abstract terms.
text.formatted: Construal Level Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Trope & Liberman, 2010)</ref> may explain why this is the case, by proposing that information stemming from people that feel psychologically closer may be processed in more concrete and less abstract terms.

text.text: This means that stories involving protagonists that feel culturally close are likely to feel more relevant to readers and offer greater personal instrumental utility (Niehoff et al., 2024; Schulz & Tompkins, 1990).
text.formatted: This means that stories involving protagonists that feel culturally close are likely to feel more relevant to readers and offer greater personal instrumental utility <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Niehoff et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Schulz & Tompkins, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, people may be more motivated to gain a deeper understanding of such experiences and see a potential to learn something valuable (Oliver & Raney, 2011).
text.formatted: Hence, people may be more motivated to gain a deeper understanding of such experiences and see a potential to learn something valuable <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Oliver & Raney, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These effects may be particularly pronounced when the content in question is negative, due to the higher informational value provided by such content (Alves et al., 2017; Oosterwijk et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These effects may be particularly pronounced when the content in question is negative, due to the higher informational value provided by such content <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alves et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Oosterwijk et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, we could expect curiosity for others' life experiences to peak when negative content coincides with a culturally close protagonist -a combination where personal relevance, motivation for social understanding, and learning potential are high, and anticipated benefits are likely to outweigh the emotional costs of engaging with negative content.
In contrast, for culturally distant others, the benefits may seem less compelling, making the emotional burden harder to justify.

In sum, this research explores how valence and cultural distance interact to influence people's curiosity for others' life stories, with particular attention to the motivational dynamics that may drive or inhibit such curiosity in everyday contexts.

Many of the personalized stories about people's life experiences found in today's media landscapes (e.g., Experience | The Guardian, n.d.) involve extraordinary experiences that few individuals are likely to experience firsthand (e.g., a newborn kidnapped from hospital).

Similarly, previous work on morbid curiosity has largely focused on rather extreme, graphic, rare or bizarre content (e.g., bodily mutilations, violent conflicts, true crime, paranormal danger; see Harrison & Frederick, 2022; Oosterwijk, 2017; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025; Scrivner, 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, previous work on morbid curiosity has largely focused on rather extreme, graphic, rare or bizarre content (e.g., bodily mutilations, violent conflicts, true crime, paranormal danger; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Harrison & Frederick, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Oosterwijk, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Scrivner, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We, however, chose to focus on major life events to understand how events that are rare and impactful for the individual (e.g., marriage, death), but common at the societal level, may shape curiosity.

Similarly, while previous work showed that stories about culturally close others are covered more frequently on the news than stories about culturally distant others (Scherer et al., 2006), this does not necessarily imply differences in individual curiosity for such stories.
text.formatted: Similarly, while previous work showed that stories about culturally close others are covered more frequently on the news than stories about culturally distant others <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Scherer et al., 2006)</ref>, this does not necessarily imply differences in individual curiosity for such stories.

text.text: Our study addresses this by testing whether people experience different levels of curiosity when being presented with the same story shared by a culturally close versus distant other.

In Study 1, we explored how curiosity about stories of others' life events differed based on whether the story was positive or negative and whether its protagonist came from a culturally close or distant country.
Based on the literature, we were particularly interested in probing whether curiosity peaked when stories described negative life events of close others.
In Study 2, we aimed to replicate the findings from Study 1 in a larger sample, taking a confirmatory approach.
We hypothesized to observe a main effect of valence with higher curiosity for negative stories, as well as an interaction effect where curiosity peaks for negative stories of culturally close others.

In addition, we explored whether six potential motives -personal utility, learning potential, social understanding, eudaimonic experience, distress, and enjoyment -mediated any of the uncovered effects.

Study 2 was preregistered at OSF (https://osf.io/aywut/?view_only=c1dbc09214664bc8a4b251bd6e01faf1) on 2023-11-20, prior to data collection, and included study design, planned sample size, exclusion criteria, planned analyses, and predictions for a main effect of valence and interaction effect of valence and distance.
text.formatted: Study 2 was preregistered at OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/aywut/?view_only=c1dbc09214664bc8a4b251bd6e01faf1">Project Link</ref>) on 2023-11-20, prior to data collection, and included study design, planned sample size, exclusion criteria, planned analyses, and predictions for a main effect of valence and interaction effect of valence and distance.

text.text: Any deviations from the preregistered analysis plan are indicated, while the analyses following the preregistered plan are presented in the Supplemental Material.
Materials, data, code and codebook for all studies are publicly accessible at OSF (https://osf.io/aywut/?view_only=c1dbc09214664bc8a4b251bd6e01faf1).
text.formatted: Materials, data, code and codebook for all studies are publicly accessible at OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/aywut/?view_only=c1dbc09214664bc8a4b251bd6e01faf1">Project Link</ref>).

text.text: Across both studies, we report all manipulations, measures, and exclusions.
In Study 1, we manipulated story valence and cultural distance to measure how these variables impact curiosity about others' stories.

Following a 2 (positive versus negative valence) x 2 (high versus low cultural distance) within-subject design, we fully counterbalanced all aspects of the design across a total of 36 trials (9 per condition) per participant (see Supplemental Figure 1).
text.formatted: Following a 2 (positive versus negative valence) x 2 (high versus low cultural distance) within-subject design, we fully counterbalanced all aspects of the design across a total of 36 trials (9 per condition) per participant (see Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants were restricted to be aged 18-65, located in the UK, with English as their first language and with a submission-quality rejection rate of below 5 percent across their previous research participations on Prolific.
Additionally, an equal gender ratio was ensured.

With no previous data on which to base the effect size assumptions, we assessed the sample size required for a within-factor repeated-measures ANOVA to detect a small effect of f(U) = 0.2 with high power (.95) at a 5% level of significance using G*Power (Version 3.1, Faul et al., 2007), which was 146.
text.formatted: With no previous data on which to base the effect size assumptions, we assessed the sample size required for a within-factor repeated-measures ANOVA to detect a small effect of f(U) = 0.2 with high power (.95) at a 5% level of significance using G*Power (Version 3.1, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Faul et al., 2007)</ref>, which was 146.

text.text: Following this, we recruited 149 participants (49.7% female, 49.7% male, 0.7% other; Mage = 39.2, SDage = 13.5; 6.7% Asian, 4.7% Black, 2.7% mixed, and 81.2% White in terms of ethnicity) through Prolific.

Participants were shown headlines describing positive or negative life stories about other people, along with maps indicating the country of origin (high or low in cultural distance) of the story's protagonist.
They were asked to rate their curiosity about each story.
After rating all the stories, the headlines were displayed again, and participants were asked to rate the story's valence and the cultural distance of the protagonist (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: After rating all the stories, the headlines were displayed again, and participants were asked to rate the story's valence and the cultural distance of the protagonist (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants were not provided with the actual stories.
Finally, participants filled out the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR, Kashdan et al., 2020), included for exploratory purposes, and provided demographical information (gender, age).
text.formatted: Finally, participants filled out the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kashdan et al., 2020)</ref>, included for exploratory purposes, and provided demographical information (gender, age).

text.text: After completion (approx. 15 minutes), participants received £1.50 as compensation.
Data collection was completed from January 12 to February 10, 2023.
Study 1 was approved by the ethical committee of the second author's institution; all participants gave informed consent.
Valence was manipulated through the story headline describing the life event.
We presented 18 positive (e.g., "How she got married on a sunny day surrounded by her family") and 18 negative headlines ("How she sat with her father when he died after a long sickness ").

Life events were taken from the Encyclopedia of Quality of Life and Well-Being Research (Mandemakers, 2014), which defines life events as "major events that occur in people's life, which alter their role, position and/or resources" (p. 3569) and provides a list of commonly encountered events.
text.formatted: Life events were taken from the Encyclopedia of Quality of Life and Well-Being Research <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Mandemakers, 2014)</ref>, which defines life events as "major events that occur in people's life, which alter their role, position and/or resources" (p. 3569) and provides a list of commonly encountered events.

text.text: Cultural distance was manipulated by presenting a world map (created with mapchart.net) alongside the headline, which visually and verbally indicated the place of origin of the story as a country either culturally close (e.g., Canada) or distant (e.g., Iraq) to the UK.

Countries were selected based on Muthukrishna and colleagues' (2020) cultural distance indicator, which quantifies the difference between any two countries using a cultural fixation index (0 for maximum closeness, 1 for maximum distance) calculated from combined data from two World Values Survey waves.
Countries culturally close to the UK (since data was 0 100 How negative or positive do you think the story will be?
0 100 How curious are you about this story?
0 100 How culturally close or distant does the person in the story feel to you?

collected with a UK sample) included Australia, Canada, Finland, France, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States, for which the cultural fixation index ranged from 0.02 to 0.04 (all bottom quartile of scale).
Culturally distant countries included Ethiopia, Georgia, Ghana, Jordan, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Rwanda, and Thailand, for which the index ranged from 0.19 to 0.34 (all top quartile of scale).
Each country was paired once with a positive, and once with a negative headline.

To counterbalance potential country-or storyspecific effects, participants were randomly assigned to one of four combination sets, which varied the country-story-pairings (for a visualization, see Supplemental Figure 1).
text.formatted: To counterbalance potential country-or storyspecific effects, participants were randomly assigned to one of four combination sets, which varied the country-story-pairings (for a visualization, see Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Our main dependent variable of interest was curiosity, which was rated using a slider scale from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely) following the question "How curious are you about this story?".
To check the effectiveness of our manipulations, we also measured perceived valence with "How negative or positive do you think the story will be?"
on a slider from 0 (extremely negative) to 100 (extremely positive) and perceived cultural distance with "How close or distant does the person in the story feel to you?"
on a slider from 0 (extremely close) to 100 (extremely distant).
This was done in a separate block, after all headlines had previously been rated on curiosity.
For the curiosity rating, the slider started at 0, for the manipulation checks at 50.

Given that our experimental conditions were fully counterbalanced, we aggregated all outcome measures (i.e., curiosity ratings and manipulation check ratings) across trials within condition per participant, such that we obtained one score for each participant per each of the four experimental conditions.

text.text: In Study 1, we leveraged a newly designed paradigm to elicit state social curiosity while systematically manipulating valence and cultural distance as situational predictors.

We established the effectiveness of our manipulations with successful manipulation checks, and the validity of our social curiosity operationalization via significant trait social curiosity correlations that are comparable in size to previously demonstrated trait-state curiosity relationships (see Litman et al., 2005).

text.text: Study 1 demonstrated a significant main effect of valence, with overall higher curiosity for negative rather than positive stories.
A main effect of cultural distance by which stories of close others would elicit higher curiosity than those of distant others was not significant.

Lastly, we found a significant interaction between valence and cultural distance on curiosity, such that curiosity was higher for negative stories from culturally close others, as opposed to all other stories.

In Study 2, we set out to test, in a confirmatory fashion (Ledgerwood, 2019; Wagenmakers et al., 2012), whether these effects replicate in a larger sample, and to explore potential mediating factors which contribute to the observed increased curiosity for negative stories of close others.

For the main effect of cultural distance, a significant indirect effect emerged only through personal utility.

Finally, for the valence-distance interaction effect on curiosity (contrast-coded for the negative, close condition), significant indirect effects emerged through personal utility, social understanding, learning potential, distress, and enjoyment.

These separate mediation analyses provided initial evidence that several of the measured mediators contributed to the relationships between valence, cultural distance, their interaction, and curiosity.

However, because each mediator and experimental effect was examined separately, the analyses did not account for shared variance among mediators or allowed us to disentangle which mediators was primarily driving which effect.
Therefore, we made two key adjustments to our analysis plan.
First, we ran a principal component analysis (PCA) on the mediators using the 'prcomp' function of the R package "stats" (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, 2024).
This allowed us to reduce dimensionality from six mediators to three, while retaining components that explained the most variance.
Second, instead of separate models, we report results of structural equation modelling with the R package "lavaan" (Rosseel, 2012).

text.text: The first component showed high loadings for personal utility (.86), social understanding (.89), learning potential (.95), and eudaimonic experience (.90) and explained 61% of the variance.
The remaining 24% of variance were explained by the second component which showed high opposing loadings for enjoyment (-.90) and distress (.77).

Consequently, we created a composite score by averaging across personal utility, social understanding, learning potential, and eudaimonic experience to reflect the first component, which we interpreted as representing 'insight'.
The remaining two variables distress and enjoyment loaded oppositely on the second component, while both positively correlated with the outcome variable curiosity.
Therefore, we retained them separately.

We defined a mediated moderation model in which curiosity was regressed on the predictor's valence (coded -0.5 for negative, 0.5 for positive), cultural distance (coded -0.5 for close, 0.5 for distant), and their interaction term.

Next to direct effects of these predictors on curiosity the model included indirect effects via three parallel mediators: insight (i.e., the composite score reflecting the first component from the PCA), enjoyment, and distress.
We defined indirect effects using the product method (i.e., multiplying the predictor-mediator and mediator-outcome paths) and accounted for residual covariances between all mediators.
For readability, insignificant paths were dropped (full results in Table 2).

text.text: After inclusion of the mediators, the total effect decomposed into two significant direct effects on curiosity and four significant indirect effects.

Two of the indirect effects, via higher insight, b = -2.77, p < .001, 95% CI [-3.53, -2.01], and via higher distress, b = -5.49, p = .001, 95% CI [-8.78, -2.20], explained the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity.

text.text: This means that people anticipated greater insight and greater distress from negative stories, with both relating to higher curiosity.
A third indirect effect between valence and curiosity, however, ran counter to this pattern.
The pathway via enjoyment was positive, b = 8.32, p < .001, 95% CI [6.34, 10.30], and thus attenuated the overall negative relationship between valence and curiosity.

text.text: As negative stories were anticipated to be enjoyed less, and enjoyment related positively to curiosity, this pathway decreased curiosity for negative stories.

After accounting for the above three indirect effects, valence did not directly link to curiosity anymore, b = -2.54, p = .062, 95% CI [-5.22, 0.13], which indicates that greater anticipated insight and -counterintuitively at first sight -greater anticipated distress fully account for higher curiosity observed for negative stories.

As for the relationship between cultural distance and curiosity, only a positive indirect effect emerged for distress, b = 0.17, p = .016, 95% CI [0.03, 0.31], which contrasted the total negative relationship between distance and curiosity.
Despite observing lower curiosity for stories about distant others, people anticipated greater distress from such stories, and greater distress positively related to curiosity.

Since this indirect effect operated in the opposite direction of the total effect, accounting for it did not alter the significance of the direct effect of distance on curiosity, b = -1.54, p < .001, 95% CI [-2.24, -0.83].

text.text: Hence, none of the captured mediators were able to explain why stories about close others elicited higher curiosity.

No indirect effects were observed for the relationship between the valence-distance interaction and curiosity, and the direct effect remained significant after inclusion of all mediators, b = 0.97, p = .003, 95% CI [0.32, 1.62].

This indicates that none of the captured mediators were able to explain why curiosity peaks when negative stories are about close others, beyond what can be explained via the valence-curiosity relationship.

Across two studies, we investigated whether people are curious about others' life stories, whether this curiosity depends on the story's valence or the cultural distance to its protagonist, and if so why.

Consistently, we found that stories about negative life events (e.g., death, illness, financial loss) elicited more curiosity than stories about positive life events (e.g., birth, marriage, career progression), and that curiosity peaked for negative stories about culturally close others.

With higher power in Study 2, we also uncovered a main effect of cultural distance such that people generally experienced more curiosity for stories about culturally close rather than distant others (a post-hoc power analysis indicated that Study 1 was underpowered with only 25% power to detect an effect of such size).
Finally, Study 2 indicated that people were more curious about negative stories, as they anticipated to gain more insight and to feel greater distress through engaging with these stories.

Combined, these mediating pathways outweighed a simultaneous counteracting path that attenuated curiosity for negative stories via lower enjoyment, with all three together fully explaining the valencecuriosity relationship.
Thus, expectations of greater insight and distress can be interpreted as 'pull factors', which increase people's curiosity for negative stories about others' experiences.
These 'pull factors' outweigh the 'push factor' of lower enjoyment of negative stories, which reduces curiosity.
Our research advances the curiosity field in several ways.
We developed the first (to the best of our knowledge) experimental paradigm that systematically varied valence and cultural distance as situational predictors of social curiosity.
We showed that both factors interacted to shape curiosity about others' life stories, such that people were most curious about negative stories from culturally close others.

The pattern mirrors well-known media dynamics, such as disproportionate news coverage of disasters in culturally closer countries, even when events of equal or greater magnitude occur elsewhere (e.g., Goldhill, 2017).
text.formatted: The pattern mirrors well-known media dynamics, such as disproportionate news coverage of disasters in culturally closer countries, even when events of equal or greater magnitude occur elsewhere (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Goldhill, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, our findings suggest this pattern cannot be explained solely by greater availability of such stories in news outlets.
When participants encountered the same story attributed to either a culturally close or distant person, their curiosity differed significantly, indicating that the bias also reflects audience demand.
Greater curiosity for negative stories is also consistent with the well-documented negativity bias, or the stronger impact of negative relative to positive events (Baumeister et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Greater curiosity for negative stories is also consistent with the well-documented negativity bias, or the stronger impact of negative relative to positive events <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Baumeister et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings, however, extend this literature in important ways.
Rather than examining how negative information is processed once encountered, we focus on the motivational stage by assessing when and why people engage with such information in the first place.

In addition, by introducing cultural distance as a situational moderator, and by identifying multiple psychological motives underlying curiosity for negative content, our work highlights important boundary conditions and underlying mechanisms of this effect.

Finally, while prior research has often emphasized extreme and rare experiences, whether in personalized news (e.g., Experience | The Guardian, n.d.) or in work on morbid curiosity (e.g., Oosterwijk, 2017), our findings show that this curiosity extends to common life events (e.g., divorce, illness, birth).

text.text: This is particularly noteworthy given the established role of novelty in curiosity (Kashdan & Silvia, 2009): Our results may suggest that content need not be objectively novel at the societal level, but rather subjectively novel to the individual to elicit curiosity.

text.text: Second, the present work supports the conceptualization of curiosity as a cost-benefit tradeoff, in which individuals weigh motives that promote or hinder engagement (Niehoff & Oosterwijk, 2020).

text.text: Our paradigm demonstrates that predictions about the psychological impact of engagement can effectively capture such motives.
One of the anticipated benefits that promotes engagement with stories about others was the potential to gain insights.
Specifically, we found people to be more curious about negative stories because they anticipated gaining more insights from engaging with them.

In this context, insight refers to anticipations of personal instrumental value for the future, increased understanding of others, learning about the world, or eudaimonic experiences (for a similar finding, see Vivanco Carlevari et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In this context, insight refers to anticipations of personal instrumental value for the future, increased understanding of others, learning about the world, or eudaimonic experiences (for a similar finding, see Vivanco <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Carlevari et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This aligns with prior work highlighting the role of epistemic value and meaning-making in motivating curiosity (Kidd & Hayden, 2015; Litman, 2005).
text.formatted: This aligns with prior work highlighting the role of epistemic value and meaning-making in motivating curiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kidd & Hayden, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Litman, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, insight was not found to mediate the relationship between cultural distance and curiosity, suggesting that people can derive insight from content involving both close and distant others.
When it comes to the anticipated emotional impact of reading about others' life events, the distinction between benefit and cost becomes more complex.
At a zero-order level, although negatively correlated with each other, both anticipated enjoyment as well as distress showed positive relationships with curiosity.

This was true for both negative and positive stories, indicating that the relationship goes beyond a simple emotional alignment of positive content with positive affect and negative content with negative affect.
At the same time, and in line with previous research, we found that negative stories were associated with anticipations of lower positive and greater negative affect (Schmidt et al., 2023).
text.formatted: At the same time, and in line with previous research, we found that negative stories were associated with anticipations of lower positive and greater negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Schmidt et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, by showing that people were more curious to read negative as opposed to positive life stories of others, our findings add to a growing body of literature disputing the claim that humans always seek out positive and avoid negative affect (Bench & Lench, 2019; Oosterwijk et al., 2020; Sharot & Sunstein, 2020).
text.formatted: Thus, by showing that people were more curious to read negative as opposed to positive life stories of others, our findings add to a growing body of literature disputing the claim that humans always seek out positive and avoid negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bench & Lench, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Oosterwijk et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Sharot & Sunstein, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, we found that anticipated distress mediated the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity.
Importantly, this effect held regardless of the cultural distance to the stories' protagonist and even when controlling for the expectation that negative stories would offer more insight.
This finding challenges the assumption that any level of negative emotions like distress are perceived as costs.

With average distress ratings ranging between 8.19 and 51.30 (out of 100) for positive and negative stories respectively, distress was anticipated to be experienced at a low to moderate rather than high level.
At these levels, we found that anticipated distress positively predicted curiosity in a linear fashion.
Because our stories did not cover extreme high levels of distress, it remains unclear whether this positive relationship would persist at higher levels.
One possibility is that only moderate distress may be experienced as functional or beneficial and thereby driving curiosity.

Support for this comes from existing literature proposing an optimal level of stress (Sapolsky, 2015), where stress impacts brain and behavior in an "inverted-U" shape, with low intensity stress yielding positive effects.
text.formatted: Support for this comes from existing literature proposing an optimal level of stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Sapolsky, 2015)</ref>, where stress impacts brain and behavior in an "inverted-U" shape, with low intensity stress yielding positive effects.

text.text: The idea is also not new to the emotion or information-seeking literature (e.g., Berlyne et al., 1966).
text.formatted: The idea is also not new to the emotion or information-seeking literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Berlyne et al., 1966)</ref>.

text.text: In a study on decisions to read negative COVID-19 news, Niehoff and colleagues (2024) found reading choice probabilities to be highest when readers anticipated feeling moderate levels of difficult emotions.

This aligns with the idea that people sometimes seek out negative emotions (Menninghaus et al., 2017; Tamir, 2016) -a behavior that may depend on anticipated coping skills (Gruber & Ranganath, 2019) and is thought to have beneficial effects on emotion regulation skills (Barrett et al., 2001; Tamir, 2009).
text.formatted: This aligns with the idea that people sometimes seek out negative emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Menninghaus et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Tamir, 2016)</ref> -a behavior that may depend on anticipated coping skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gruber & Ranganath, 2019)</ref> and is thought to have beneficial effects on emotion regulation skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Tamir, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, with scores ranging between 11.78 and 12.48 (out of 100), we observed low levels of enjoyment for both negative stories about culturally close as well as distant protagonist.

This finding challenges persistent theories proposing that curiosity for negative content is driven by pleasure related to downward comparison against outgroups (i.e., Schadenfreude, Ouwerkerk et al., 2018) or gratitude for one's own situation (Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This finding challenges persistent theories proposing that curiosity for negative content is driven by pleasure related to downward comparison against outgroups (i.e., Schadenfreude, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Ouwerkerk et al., 2018)</ref> or gratitude for one's own situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It also indicates that benign masochism (Rozin et al., 2013) did not play a role in driving the observed heightened curiosity for negative stories.
text.formatted: It also indicates that benign masochism <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Rozin et al., 2013)</ref> did not play a role in driving the observed heightened curiosity for negative stories.

text.text: While enjoyment positively correlated with curiosity, we found a significant indirect effect of enjoyment in suppressing curiosity for negative stories.
Lastly, our research advances the curiosity field by focusing on a currently underexplored facet: social curiosity.

While previous research has examined social curiosity as a trait through self-report questionnaires (e.g., Kashdan et al., 2020; Litman & Pezzo, 2007), our studies examined it as a situational experience elicited by social stimuli.
text.formatted: While previous research has examined social curiosity as a trait through self-report questionnaires (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kashdan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Litman & Pezzo, 2007)</ref>, our studies examined it as a situational experience elicited by social stimuli.

text.text: This aligns with definitions of social curiosity as curiosity for information about people (Litman et al., 2005) and is consistent with similar approaches used to study domain-specific forms of curiosity (e.g., morbid curiosity; Oosterwijk, 2017).
text.formatted: This aligns with definitions of social curiosity as curiosity for information about people <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Litman et al., 2005)</ref> and is consistent with similar approaches used to study domain-specific forms of curiosity (e.g., morbid curiosity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Oosterwijk, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although such situational responses may partly reflect overlapping forms of curiosity (e.g., epistemic or morbid curiosity) or related motivations, our paradigm was designed to primarily capture curiosity for social information.

The validity of this approach is highlighted by small to moderate correlations observed between participants' situational social curiosity ratings and their trait social curiosity, indicating that state and trait manifestations of curiosity are related but distinct constructs.
Therefore, our research suggests that a full understanding of social curiosity cannot be achieved by focusing on individual differences only.
This insight can contribute to ongoing debates in curiosity research about the relationship between trait and state curiosity (Jach et al., 2024; Peterson & Hidi, 2019).
text.formatted: This insight can contribute to ongoing debates in curiosity research about the relationship between trait and state curiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Jach et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Peterson & Hidi, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While our findings advance our understanding of the mechanisms linking valence, cultural distance, and curiosity, in part even fully explaining the relationship between valence and curiosity through anticipated insight and affective impact, it is important to note that not all analyses were conducted in a confirmatory fashion.
The mediation analysis was exploratory, with only the research question and an analysis plan but not the hypotheses preregistered.
In addition, the mediators captured in this research were less suited to explain why people were more curious about stories about close others.
In fact, the only observed indirect effect for cultural distance was a pathway that ran counter the total effect via lower anticipated distress for stories of close others.
However, the significant distance main effect as well as interaction effect suggest that additional processes may contribute to this pattern, which could be explored in future research.
One such process could be related to motivated empathy (Zaki, 2014).
text.formatted: One such process could be related to motivated empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Zaki, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: As people feel more motivated to foster social identification with culturally close others, showing empathy in the face of negative experiences may be a way of doing so (Cameron et al., 2022; Jami et al., 2024).
text.formatted: As people feel more motivated to foster social identification with culturally close others, showing empathy in the face of negative experiences may be a way of doing so <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cameron et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Jami et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, experiences of close others may be easier to understand, process, or relate to, making it less effortful to read stories about them (Inzlicht et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, experiences of close others may be easier to understand, process, or relate to, making it less effortful to read stories about them <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Inzlicht et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: It could also be that a sense of moral obligation to engage within particular -negative information may be stronger for culturally close compared to distant others (Hoffner et al., 2009).
text.formatted: It could also be that a sense of moral obligation to engage within particular -negative information may be stronger for culturally close compared to distant others <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hoffner et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: We recommend that future research include motivated empathy as well as effortfulness as potential mediating mechanisms that may underlie the role of cultural distance and its interaction with valence in driving curiosity, and to test all potential mediators in a confirmatory way.
In addition, we encourage future work to more precisely examine the role of anticipated distress in the positive association between negative valence and curiosity.
Our results point to a potential inverted U-shaped relationship, in which curiosity peaks at moderate levels of anticipated distress.
To better understand this dynamic, we suggest two directions for future work.

First, researchers could manipulate anticipated distress along a continuous spectrum to determine how varying levels influence curiosity across its full range, rather than relying on categorical contrasts between negative and positive content.
Second, our study did not clearly distinguish between negative affect and arousal.
Because arousal is known to increase the social transmission of information regardless of valence (Berger, 2011), it may also underlie heightened curiosity toward distressing content.
text.formatted: Because arousal is known to increase the social transmission of information regardless of valence <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berger, 2011)</ref>, it may also underlie heightened curiosity toward distressing content.

text.text: Future research should disentangle the effects of negative affect and arousal to test this possibility.
Together, these approaches could help clarify when negative feelings are perceived as costs versus motivational benefits, and how mixed-valence content shapes curiosity.
Furthermore, future work may address some of our methodological limitations.

To vary cultural distance within our stimuli, stories presented to participants were described as either stemming from a country with low or high cultural distance to the UK, according to Muthukrishna and colleagues' (2020) cultural distance indicator.
Therefore, the generalizability of our findings beyond the UK-context should be confirmed with future research deploying the paradigm using different countries.
In addition, it is plausible that our selected countries differed on further dimensions, such as political or economic distance, possibly introducing confounding factors.
For future research, we thus suggest disentangling these factors by including separate continuous measures of each distance into the model.
This would facilitate an evaluation of the relative influence of each dimension in driving social curiosity.
It is relevant to note that the observed effect sizes across both studies are small.

For the main and interaction effects in Study 1, this is partially due to the cost-benefit-analysis underlying curiosity for negative content, as reflected in the mixed mediating and suppressing mechanisms uncovered in Study 2.
It is not uncommon for individual contributions of mediators to be small when several factors underlie a mechanism (Bonanno et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It is not uncommon for individual contributions of mediators to be small when several factors underlie a mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bonanno et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, when accumulated across many situations, such as the ubiquitous exposure to information about others' experiences, even small effects can have a significant impact (Götz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, when accumulated across many situations, such as the ubiquitous exposure to information about others' experiences, even small effects can have a significant impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Götz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, we encourage future research to conceptually replicate the above findings using different materials (e.g., different headlines and countries) or different operationalizations of valence and cultural distance.
Finally, researchers may explore related but distinct questions.
While we conceptualize social curiosity as curiosity about social stimuli, an important extension is curiosity as a social mechanism -that is, how it unfolds within and motivates interaction.
This shifts the focus from non-interactive information seeking to curiosity as a relational process.

Such questions could be examined in real-time using dyadic interaction paradigms, where curiosity is observed behaviorally (e.g., question-asking, follow-up responses), or operationalized in everyday behavior (e.g., willingness to initiate conversations, digital communication patterns).
This approach aligns with calls to move social psychological research beyond the laboratory and into naturalistic contexts (Holleman et al., 2020; Risko et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This approach aligns with calls to move social psychological research beyond the laboratory and into naturalistic contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Holleman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Risko et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to advancing the field of curiosity and providing avenues for future research, the above findings carry practical implications on how to use personal stories about strangers to encourage people to engage with others' perspectives.

For example, these insights may prove useful to NGOs and charities seeking to enhance engagement with their content and promote pro-social behavior -whether by highlighting similarities between the story protagonist and the audience or by emphasizing the potential for gaining insights.
They could also provide journalistic outlets knowledge on how to manage news fatigue, such as including personal stories of culturally close others (Maier et al., 2017).
text.formatted: They could also provide journalistic outlets knowledge on how to manage news fatigue, such as including personal stories of culturally close others <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Maier et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, understanding the psychological mechanisms that drive curiosity about others offers valuable tools for fostering empathy, perspective-taking, and social connection in an increasingly fragmented world.
